BDRY: Not a stock fund at all: it holds futures on shipping rates for bulk carriers, the giant ships that move coal, grain and iron ore. Its value jumps with global freight costs, making it a volatile bet tied to world trade rather than to company profits.
PBMR: Options on the S&P 500 designed to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in March, the deep protection its Buffer 20 name describes. The price of that safety is a cap on gains when markets climb strongly.
DYLD: A go-anywhere income fund holding many kinds of debt at once: company bonds, government debt, bank loans, mortgage securities and even private loans. The dynamic approach shifts the mix toward wherever yields look most worth the risk, so its character changes over time.
NUSA: Short-term US bonds that pass environmental, social and governance screens: Treasuries, government-backed bonds and company debt all due within about five years. Short maturities keep price swings small, so it is a cautious income holding for investors who want ESG rules applied to bonds.
SPDF: Large US stocks bought through a broad index fund, with a technical risk overlay that can pull money out when market signals turn bad. The defender design aims to sidestep deep crashes, though the signals can also pull it out just before rebounds.
RMME: A money market fund holding only cash, US government securities and loans backed by them, all maturing within about a year. It aims to keep a steady one dollar share price and pay modest interest, the lowest-risk corner of the fund world.
WAR: Companies selling technology to militaries: drones, satellites, cybersecurity, chips and aerospace systems, split between tech and defense industry names. It is a focused bet on defense spending in a dangerous world, and its smaller, specialized firms make it swing more than big defense funds.
PTEU: Big Eurozone companies, banks, industrial and energy firms among them, with a trend rule that can move half or all of the money into Treasury bills when European stocks fall. The Trendpilot switch aims to dodge long slumps, at the risk of rejoining rallies late.
FDAT: A fund of other funds that moves between stock funds, high yield bond funds and cash as its managers judge the market's mood. It was sitting mostly in cash-like holdings at the last look, which shows how defensive this tactical fund can turn.
FMNY: Bonds from New York governments and public agencies, from the state dormitory authority to power and convention center issuers, including lower-rated ones for extra yield. The interest dodges federal, New York State and New York City taxes, making it a New Yorker's income fund.
DECM: Options on the S&P 500 chasing the deepest available loss protection over a year starting in December, true to the Max Buffer label. With protection pushed to the max, only a small cap of gains remains, so it is about keeping money, not growing it fast.
INOV: Options tied to a fund of large companies in developed overseas markets, with a power buffer against part of any loss over a period resetting each November. It softens the bumps of foreign investing while capping the gains, and results depend on the full period.
SPYH: The actual stocks of the S&P 500, paired with an options collar that buys downside protection and sells calls to pay for it and add income. The hedge trims both ways: smaller losses in falls, smaller gains in rallies, plus extra income along the way.
TMFX: Mid-sized and smaller US companies that Motley Fool analysts have recommended in their newsletters, spread across technology, health care and industry. It packages the Fool's next-wave picks after its best-known recommendations, so it is more speculative than its flagship fund.
RJMI: Municipal bonds from states, cities, schools and public agencies across the US, picked actively by Raymond James for tax-free income. The interest escapes federal income tax, and the active approach hunts for value among thousands of small local issuers.
FBDC: Business development companies and specialty lenders, the firms that lend to mid-sized private companies and pass most earnings out as dividends. It is an income fund built on private credit, with high payouts and the risk that borrowers struggle in a downturn.
SAMM: Stocks chosen with a macro lens by Strategas, tilting toward whatever parts of the market its research sees as having momentum, currently technology and health care. The willingness to roam across company types, even other funds and partnerships, makes it a flexible all-in-one equity bet.
ARMW: Built around one stock, Arm Holdings, the chip designer, using swaps to deliver about 120 percent of its weekly move plus weekly income payments. Everything depends on a single, richly priced chip stock, so it is a short-term trading tool with big swings.
BCSM: Small and mid-sized companies picked by Baron for long-term growth, led by technology, industrial and health care names. Baron's patient style holds growers for years, so the fund rides these younger companies through their ups and downs rather than trading around them.
ENRG: Companies that explore for, produce and deliver oil, gas, coal and uranium around the world, gathered under a North American energy independence theme. It is a full-throated fossil fuel and nuclear fuel bet, swinging with energy prices and drilling activity.
CPSF: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to shield against losses over an outcome period that resets each February, with gains limited to pay for the shield. It is meant to be bought and held for the whole period, when the protection works as designed.
FSZ: Swiss companies chosen by a scoring system that favors growth and value signals, spanning drug makers, industrial firms and big banks. It is a single-country fund on one of the world's richest, most stable markets, with returns also riding the Swiss franc.
CPRY: Options on a small company index fund, structured to protect against losses over an outcome period that resets each January, with a cap on gains as the trade. It brings a safety net to the wildest corner of the stock market, small company shares.
AUGT: Options on large US stocks that take the first 10% of a market loss over a year starting in August, the Buffer10 promise in its name. A moderate shield like this keeps more upside than deep buffers, though gains are still capped.
LLDR: US Treasury bonds in a ladder stretching from ten to thirty years, with slices maturing steadily along the way. Long government bonds pay dependable income and often rally when stocks crash, but their prices sink hard when long-term rates rise.
MARU: Options on the S&P 500 set to absorb the first part of a market drop over a one-year period starting in March, with a 15% buffer in the design. Unlike capped buffers, gains beyond a small starting spread are unlimited, the feature in its Uncapped name.
FKU: British companies picked by a scoring method hunting for growth and value, led by banks, consumer and industrial firms. It tilts away from the UK's giant global names toward mid-sized domestic businesses, so it leans more on Britain's own economy and the pound.
XLYI: The consumer discretionary slice of the S&P 500: retailers, restaurants, car makers and travel companies, held through the sector's big fund with options sold for premium income. It lives and dies by consumer spending, with the premiums adding a payout on top.
DDTY: A fund built to gain in two directions: it holds a big US stock fund plus options designed to profit from moderate falls as well as rises, with a 10% buffer as the name indicates. Big moves either way can break the design, so it suits range-bound markets.
NOVP: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb about the first eighth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in November, per the Buffer 12 name. It is a middle-ground buffer: less protection than the deep versions, more room to gain than they allow.
THOR: Dividend-paying companies from around the world, including phone companies, banks, preferred shares and property trusts, plus other income-paying instruments. It builds income from many sources at once, favoring steady global payers over chasing the single highest yield.
SUIS: This trust holds SUI, the token of the Sui blockchain, and stakes it to earn additional tokens as rewards. Like other single-coin funds, its price is simply the coin's price, with all the sharp rises and crashes that crypto brings.
DDFG: A stock fund plus layered options designed to return gains whether the market rises or falls moderately, with a 15% buffer behind it, as the name says. The dual direction trick works only within limits: a plunge or a surge beyond the design undoes it.
NRES: Companies that dig, drill and grow the world's raw materials: miners, oil and gas producers, fertilizer and timber firms from many countries. It is a bet on commodity demand and inflation, since resource stocks often rise when the prices of what they produce climb.
EMET: Miners of copper and the other metals that electrification runs on, from global mining giants to smaller copper specialists. It is a focused wager on the buildout of power grids, electric vehicles and data centers, and metal prices make it volatile.
TUG: A tactical growth fund that shifts between Nasdaq-style growth stocks, long-term Treasury bonds and cash-like bills as conditions change. The switching is the strategy: lean into growth when it works, hide in bonds or bills when it does not.
NFLY: A single-stock income fund built on Netflix: options mimic owning the shares while covered calls are sold against them for income. The sold calls cap the upside, so it harvests the streaming giant's swings as income rather than riding its full growth.
IDX: Indonesia's listed companies, led by its big banks, with miners, energy firms and the national phone company behind them. It is a single-country bet on Southeast Asia's biggest economy, bringing currency risk and emerging market swings with it.
ESSC: Small US companies spread evenly across health care, technology, banks and industry, picked with Eventide's values-based research. Small firms offer more room to grow and more risk, and the values screen rules out businesses the managers see as harming people.
ISWN: About nine tenths sits in US Treasuries, while roughly a tenth buys long-dated call options on developed overseas stocks. The BlackSwan design protects most of the money while keeping a leveraged ticket on foreign markets, so gains can surprise in strong years.
VNAM: Vietnamese companies across property, banking, industry and consumer goods, the whole young stock market of a fast-growing frontier economy. One giant conglomerate dominates the market's value, so the fund leans heavily on it, and frontier markets bring extra political and currency risk.
QPX: A dynamic fund of funds that rotates among stock funds, bond funds, gold and even volatility products as its managers chase growth. At the last look it leaned on technology funds and gold, a mix that shows how far this flexible fund can roam.
BWQG: Companies the managers believe can grow faster than average for a long time, led by technology and internet names. It is a concentrated growth portfolio, mostly direct stocks with some index fund ballast, and growth stocks swing harder than the broad market.
CAAA: The top-rated slices of commercial mortgage securities: loans on malls, offices, hotels and other business properties, all carrying AAA ratings at purchase. It aims for bond income a notch above Treasuries with the highest-rated protection in commercial property debt.
BSR: A fund of funds built mainly from big US index funds and sector funds, adjusted under Beacon's unified catalyst approach. Its top layer is plain large-company exposure, with tactical tilts around the edges that try to catch turning points in the market.
CCEF: Closed-end income funds bought when they trade below the value of what they own, so the fund collects their payouts plus any discount that closes. Calamos hunts this arbitrage across dozens of CEFs, making income with a value twist rather than from bonds directly.
HRSK: Large US stock exposure built from index futures, funds and shares, with an active hedging program meant to cut losses in market falls. Toews built its name on avoiding deep drawdowns, so the fund accepts some cost and lag in rallies as insurance.
NVBU: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to absorb the first part of a market loss over a one-year period starting in November, with a 15% buffer in the build. Gains past a starting spread are uncapped, so it keeps more of a rally than capped buffers do.
MMID: Mid-sized US companies spread widely across industry, technology, finance and health care, picked actively by MFS. Mid-caps are the market's middle children: more established than small firms, more room to grow than giants, and this fund spreads its bets broadly among them.
WUGI: Companies building or benefiting from the 5G digital economy, heavily weighted to chip makers and the equipment behind fast networks. It is a theme bet on connected everything, from phones to factories, and its chip concentration makes it swing with the semiconductor cycle.
